title: The Path to Power
hook: A faster lab can still be defenseless if the launch budget never buys a barrier.
counterintuition: Better execution can still leave the company exposed; instead, the path to power starts with invention or a crux choice that changes what rivals must overcome.
tryThisNow: Take one initiative and label it operational excellence, invention, or crux choice. Fund it as strategy only if it can plausibly create a barrier.
keyTakeaway: The path to power runs through invention or a crux directional choice that can create a barrier before operational excellence scales the chosen model.

breakdown.fastRead:
You can make the lab faster tomorrow and still own nothing defensible. Megan stands over a launch budget, a turnaround chart, and an at-home sample kit prototype. One option improves the existing lab. The other might change how customers enter the system.

The path to power is not better execution piled on a me-too position. Operational excellence matters, but it is not strategy by itself. Me-too work can be polished and still powerless, because no rival has been forced into a worse position.
breakdown.deepRead:
Megan sorts the two options before moving the budget. Faster lab service may help margins and satisfaction. The at-home collection model might create switching costs, data, density, or a new purchasing habit. The strategic question is which option can create a protected advantage, not which one looks more competent next quarter.

Operational excellence makes the chosen path work. It rarely chooses the path.

Invention matters when it opens a route to a power. It might create a business model incumbents hesitate to copy, a resource that can be cornered, a network that can start compounding, or a process that can later become embedded. Innovation language without barrier logic is just decoration.

Lars sees the same split in boat repair. A tighter repair calendar improves today. A predictive maintenance subscription could change renewal behavior and create continuity value. He pins the calendar under the sensor proposal and marks which choice can shape the future barrier.

The crux is the directional choice that makes later excellence matter.

The same discipline protects against false invention. A strange feature is not strategic because it is strange. It has to point toward scale, network value, switching costs, branding, a cornered resource, process power, or an incumbent trap. Otherwise the team has only built a harder version of me-too.
breakdown.fullRead:
Salt dries in white lines on the repair calendar above Lars's workbench. His crew can answer calls faster by reorganizing the shop. That would be useful. The sensor proposal asks for something riskier: install monitors on customer boats, detect failures early, and renew service before breakdowns happen. The second path is not automatically better. It is simply the one that might create a switching-cost route later.

A company often wants to postpone this choice. It can improve support, clean up billing, redesign the website, tune sales scripts, and hire better managers. These may all be good moves. They may also leave the company in the same strategic position: better run, easier to admire, still easy to copy.

Which initiative changes the contest if it works?

Sofia uses that question with an education publisher. The feature list is full of respectable updates. She removes every feature that merely copies the competitor catalog and leaves the adaptive practice data mockup on the table. The data feature could teach the product and raise switching costs later. The copied catalog feature may keep the company current without creating protection.

The source pressure is strict: me-too positioning is insufficient because it leaves no barrier. Matching the category standard may be necessary just to play, but it rarely creates power. You can be excellent at the same game everyone else is playing and still have no reason competitors cannot follow.

Lin faces this with an urban farming supplier. Lower-cost deliveries are attractive, but if every rival can copy the route and prices next month, the improvement remains exposed. Proprietary crop-planning software might be harder to copy if it gathers customer data, improves recommendations, and later raises switching costs. Lin writes barrier or no barrier next to each initiative before funding the neatest operational improvement.

There is a danger on the other side too. Invention for its own sake burns attention. A strange product, a new market, or a clever model is not strategic unless it points toward one of the powers. Novelty should serve barrier creation. Otherwise the company has traded me-too execution for me-too innovation language.

Daniel learns that after two perfect cybersecurity workshops. Clients liked them. Rivals could run similar workshops. His role-specific breach drill is rougher, but it creates client data fields and habits a generic course cannot easily match. The path to power begins when he stops polishing the old workshop and builds the thing that might become defensible.

Good operators still matter. Once the barrier-forming path is chosen, execution determines whether the invention survives contact with customers. But the order matters. First choose the path that can create power. Then get very good at walking it.

examples.title: Megan sorts the launch budget

planSpec.domain: specialty diagnostics startup choosing between faster lab service and a new at-home collection model
planSpec.audience: founder deciding whether better execution or invention opens the path
planSpec.stakes: faster service improves operations, but the at-home model might create switching and scale opportunities
planSpec.requiredBeat: Megan has you sort the two options into better execution and possible barrier creation before moving the launch budget.

examples.scenario: At 8:40 a.m. in a diagnostics lab conference room, Megan can make the lab faster tomorrow and still own nothing defensible. She places the launch budget between a lab turnaround chart and an at-home sample kit prototype. The chart improves what competitors already do. The kit may change how patients enter the system. Her cursor stays off the transfer button while she must decide whether to fund operational excellence or a possible path to power.
examples.whatToDo: Classify the faster lab as execution and the sample kit as a possible barrier-forming invention. Move budget only after naming which future power the chosen path could create.
examples.whyItMatters: Execution can improve a me-too position without protecting it. The strategic spend is the one that could change switching costs, scale, network, or another barrier later.

examples.title: Lars pins the sensor proposal

planSpec.domain: regional boat-repair company considering a predictive maintenance subscription
planSpec.audience: owner weighing a crux directional choice against more efficient repairs
planSpec.stakes: the subscription could change customer lock-in while faster repairs alone remain copyable
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lars pins the repair calendar under the sensor proposal and marks which choice could change the future barrier.

examples.scenario: Salt dries in white lines on the repair calendar above the workbench. Lars pins the sensor proposal beneath it and circles two choices: answer repair calls faster, or install monitors that turn breakdowns into renewals. The crew can do the first by Monday. The second changes the customer relationship. Before buying sensors, Lars must pick which path can create a barrier, not just a smoother shop.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the repair-calendar move as operational improvement and the sensor subscription as the possible crux. Choose the path only if it can build continuity value customers would not easily abandon.
examples.whyItMatters: A faster shop may still be copied. A monitored subscription could reshape renewal behavior, which gives execution a strategic path to reinforce.

examples.title: Sofia deletes the catalog copies

planSpec.domain: education publisher moving from textbook updates to adaptive practice data
planSpec.audience: product director deciding whether invention serves barrier creation
planSpec.stakes: new features matter only if they create data, switching costs, or network effects that rivals cannot easily match
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sofia asks which proposed feature creates a barrier, then removes every feature that merely copies the competitor catalog.

examples.scenario: "Which one gets harder to copy after launch?" Sofia asks, standing beside a feature list, a competitor catalog, and a practice data mockup. The team votes for six updates. She removes every feature already in the rival catalog and leaves the data loop on the table. Before the roadmap freezes, she must decide whether invention is serving barrier creation or only making the list longer.
examples.whatToDo: Cut copied catalog features from the strategy argument. Keep the adaptive data feature only if it can create learning, switching costs, or another barrier after launch.
examples.whyItMatters: New features are strategic when they change what rivals must overcome. Matching the market standard may be necessary, but it does not build power by itself.

examples.title: Lin refuses the neat delivery win

planSpec.domain: urban farming supplier choosing between lower-cost deliveries and proprietary crop-planning software
planSpec.audience: strategy lead deciding where the crux sits
planSpec.stakes: delivery excellence is useful but may not create power; the planning tool might reshape switching costs and data advantage
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lin writes barrier or no barrier next to each initiative and refuses to fund the neatest operational improvement first.

examples.scenario: Which improvement would still matter if every rival copied it next month? In a Toronto farm-supply planning room at 1:10 p.m., Lin lays an initiative list beside a crop-planning mockup and a delivery cost sheet. The delivery route saves money. The planning tool might gather farm data and guide future orders. She writes barrier or no barrier next to each line, then she must decide whether to fund the neat operational win or the rougher software experiment.
examples.whatToDo: Label each initiative by the barrier it could create. Do not fund the cleanest efficiency gain first if it leaves the supplier in the same copyable position.
examples.whyItMatters: Operational gains can be real and still exposed. The crux move is the one that could reshape data, switching, or customer behavior in a way rivals cannot instantly match.

examples.title: Daniel circles the client data fields

planSpec.domain: cybersecurity training firm inventing role-specific breach drills
planSpec.audience: founder separating product invention from polished course delivery
planSpec.stakes: the firm needs a new basis for protection, not just smoother workshops
planSpec.requiredBeat: Daniel compares the old workshop checklist with the first role-specific drill and circles the client data that could make the second defensible.

examples.scenario: It took Daniel two perfect workshops to admit perfection had no moat. Before, his checklist ran cleanly and clients applauded. After, the first role-specific breach drill produced messy but useful client data fields. He places the workshop checklist beside the drill report and circles the data that a generic training firm would not have. The renewal call now depends on whether rough invention beats polished sameness.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the old workshop as execution and the role-specific drill as the strategic candidate. Build the drill further only where client data can create learning and defensibility.
examples.whyItMatters: A perfect workshop can still be copied. The rough drill matters because it may create information and habits that make future training harder to replace.

examples.title: Camille dates the underwriting window

planSpec.domain: specialty insurer deciding whether to underwrite a new climate-risk niche
planSpec.audience: executive weighing a directional choice under market timing
planSpec.stakes: the opening may close if the firm waits until the niche is obvious and every carrier has the same data
planSpec.requiredBeat: Camille lays the flood maps over the claims file and marks the date when the niche stops being early enough to build power.

examples.scenario: The map paper buckles where Camille has spilled coffee on the coastline. In the postmortem, she lays flood maps over the claims file and an underwriting calendar, then marks the month when the niche became obvious to every carrier. The firm waited for cleaner data and lost the early learning window. Camille writes the date when operational caution stopped protecting the company and started costing it power.
examples.whatToDo: Mark the window when the niche is still early enough to build unique learning or relationships. Use operations to support that choice, not to delay until every rival sees the same opening.
examples.whyItMatters: Some paths to power require moving before the market is comfortable. Waiting for perfect execution can surrender the timing that would have made the choice defensible.

questions.prompt: A diagnostics startup can either cut lab turnaround from 36 to 24 hours or launch home sample kits that might create new patient habits. Which question best follows the path-to-power logic?
choices: Which option could create a future barrier rather than only improve the current model?
Which option is easiest to explain in a staff meeting?
Which option uses the least invention?
questions.explanation: The issue is not ease or novelty. The strategic question is which choice can create switching costs, scale, data, or another barrier that rivals must overcome.

questions.prompt: A company is excellent at the same service every rival offers. Customers are happy, but rivals can match the improvements quickly. What is missing?
choices: Operational excellence
A route from that excellence to a protected advantage
Customer satisfaction
questions.explanation: The company may be well run and liked, but power needs a barrier. The missing piece is a crux or invention that changes the contest rather than perfects sameness.

questions.prompt: An education publisher copies every rival feature and ships on time. Another proposal would gather adaptive practice data that could improve future recommendations. Which move is more strategic?
choices: The copied feature list, because matching rivals is always power
The adaptive data feature, if it can create learning or switching costs rivals lack
Neither, because education products cannot create power
questions.explanation: Copied features may be necessary but remain me-too. The data loop could become a barrier if it improves the product and makes future replacement harder.

questions.prompt: A boat-repair shop reorganizes scheduling and answers calls faster. A sensor subscription could change renewals but is harder to build. Which response is strongest?
choices: Fund only scheduling because it improves operations immediately
Evaluate the subscription as a crux path while keeping scheduling as support
Avoid both because strategy should not involve operations
questions.explanation: Scheduling helps, but the subscription may create continuity value. The best answer separates operational support from a possible barrier-forming path.

questions.prompt: A team calls a strange new feature strategic because nobody has seen it before. Customers do not value it, and it creates no cost, network, switching, brand, resource, process, or incumbent-copying barrier. What should you say?
choices: The feature is strategic because difference is always power
The feature is branding because it attracts attention
Novelty alone is not enough; invention has to serve barrier creation
questions.explanation: Invention matters when it opens a route to power. Difference without customer value or barrier logic is only novelty. Attention alone does not establish branding power.

questions.prompt: A farm-supply company can lower delivery cost this quarter or build crop-planning software that may gather customer data and guide repeat orders. What should the strategy lead mark beside each option?
choices: Whether the CEO personally prefers it
Whether it is operational excellence, invention, or a crux directional choice
Whether it can be announced before Friday
questions.explanation: The useful classification separates exposed efficiency from a possible barrier-forming path. Preference and announcement timing do not answer the strategic question.

questions.prompt: A cybersecurity training firm runs flawless generic workshops, but competitors can copy them. A role-specific drill is rough and produces client-specific data. Which risk is worth considering?
choices: The generic workshop must be strategic because it is flawless
The firm should avoid all invention until workshops are impossible to copy
The rough drill may be the better path if its data can become defensible
questions.explanation: The rough drill might create learning or switching value that generic workshops lack. Flawless execution of a copyable offer can still leave the firm exposed.

questions.prompt: An insurer waits until every data source confirms a climate-risk niche. By then all competitors have entered with similar data. What path-to-power mistake appears?
choices: The firm let operational certainty erase the timing window for a crux choice
The firm created network economies by waiting
The firm built brand power through caution
questions.explanation: Some powers require early directional choice. Waiting for perfect certainty can remove the chance to build unique learning, relationships, or position. The prompt shows no network or brand premium.

questions.prompt: A firm improves billing, support, hiring, and website speed while leaving its offer identical to every competitor. What is the best critique?
choices: These improvements may help, but they do not yet explain a protected path to power
These improvements are useless because operations never matter
These improvements automatically create process power
questions.explanation: Operations matter, but the critique is missing barrier creation. Process power would require an embedded interlocking system, not a general list of improvements.

reviewCards.front: A team is executing better than last quarter. What must you retrieve before calling that strategy?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the barrier the better execution can help create. Operational excellence supports strategy, but it does not become power without a protected path.

reviewCards.front: A polished copier service has happy customers, but every rival can match the same moves. What should you retrieve about me-too positioning?
reviewCards.back: It leaves no barrier. A rival has not been forced into a worse position, so the company may be competent and still exposed.

reviewCards.front: A product team proposes a strange feature no buyer has requested. What must you retrieve before calling the invention strategic?
reviewCards.back: When it opens a route to one of the powers: scale, network, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, or process power.

reviewCards.front: A budget can fund a faster call center or a customer-data loop. What should you retrieve to identify the crux directional choice?
reviewCards.back: It is the choice that changes which path the company can build power on. It decides where later operational excellence will compound instead of merely improve sameness.

reviewCards.front: A team waits until every competitor sees the same niche. What should you retrieve about timing risk?
reviewCards.back: Some windows close. By the time an opening is obvious, rivals may have the same information and the chance to build unique power may be gone.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use the path-to-power test before funding improvement. Classify each initiative as operational excellence, invention, or crux choice, then ask what barrier it could create.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a feature copies the category standard, then I will treat it as table stakes unless it creates a barrier rivals lack.
If two initiatives compete, then I will fund the one with a plausible route to power before the one that merely cleans current operations.
If I call something innovation, then I will name the specific power it could lead to before using that word in the plan.
If a choice depends on being early, then I will mark the date when waiting turns the option into a crowded me-too move.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one current initiative. Label it operational excellence, invention, or crux choice, then write the power it could create or admit that it is only improvement.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, review your active projects and sort them into support work, table stakes, and barrier-building bets. Move one hour toward the barrier-building bet.

memorableLines.text: You can make the lab faster tomorrow and still own nothing defensible.
memorableLines.why: It separates useful improvement from protected strategy.

memorableLines.text: Operational excellence makes the chosen path work. It rarely chooses the path.
memorableLines.why: It clarifies sequence in two plain sentences.

memorableLines.text: Which initiative changes the contest if it works?
memorableLines.why: It gives readers the chapter's core diagnostic question.
